newsitem.title: CHINA: FOCUS-China launches new share quota, markets jump.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-China launches new share quota, markets jump.

text.p: China on Monday announced a flood of new share issues in an attempt to cool the country's surging stock markets, but investors responded by driving the market up further, analysts said.
The official media announced an extra share issue quota of five billion yuan ($600 million) to be added to the 10 billion yuan already announced in late 1996.

Brokers said the move was partly aimed at throwing cold water on the country's persistently bullish markets, but also indicated growing official satisfaction with the way the equity markets have been developing.
Both the Shanghai and Shenzhen local currency A share indices jumped nearly four percent on the day. The new quota applies to the A shares only.
"You could throw garbage in front of investors right now and they'd pick it up and eat it," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai.
Li Qian, a spokeswoman for the Shanghai Stock Exchange, said the original 10 billion yuan quota announced in late 1996 had largely been used up already, and the issues had gone smoothly.
But some brokers warned poor handling of the new issues, such as a sudden rush of companies seeking to issue shares too soon, could cause the A share market to fall.
A drop in the A share market would also have a negative effect on the foreign currency B share market, they said.

"It's likely that all of this won't get out the door this year," said Alex Conroy, a Shanghai-based senior investment analyst for ING Barings. "But if they start going too fast, that will make the markets more volatile."

The move will help draw money from existing A shares into new issues later in 1997, brokers said. But the euphoric mood of the A share markets, which are currently hovering around two-year highs, will help absorb the new issues, they said.
"They announced the issue because the market is in pretty good shape right now," said an analyst at a local securities firm. "This won't have too big an effect on sentiment."
However, brokers said the market's prevailing casino mentality may yet cause Beijing to intervene to stop speculation and bring prices down.
